text:
In the last video, you learned how to review your test results,
group the mistakes you found,
and decide which problems need attention first.

That review also helps you understand the application better, so you
now have more to go on than when you chose your first test cases.
That will help you make your test set more useful.

In this video, you'll look at how to use that understanding to expand
your test coverage by looking for important situations
you haven't tested or haven't tested enough.

You'll look for real examples to add and use synthetic cases where you
still need more coverage.
And as you add cases, you'll decide which ones are worth keeping,

so you have a set you can keep running to check the behaviors
and failures you care about as you improve the application.

A good place to start is by looking through what you already have for
clues about what else to test,

such as the mistakes you found in the last video, your requirements,
and real requests or bug reports.

For example, think back to the unsafe match in the shelter app,
where a volunteer was matched with a dog they couldn't safely handle.
You can use that mistake to help you think of other cases to test.

Here, the agent approved a match it should have rejected,
so you might think about other reasons a match should be rejected.

For example, the shelter also requires volunteers to be eligible for
outings. What if the volunteer is experienced, but isn't eligible?

If you haven't tested that situation yet, it could be worth checking
whether the agent follows the eligibility rule.
You can also go back to your requirements for inspiration.

You've already used them to come up with cases,
but now you've seen what actually happened,
that list might help you think of situations you missed.

Also, don't skip a requirement just because all of
your test cases passed.

You could take one of those cases and change a detail that matters
for the requirement.

Think about what the agent should do with that change,
and you have another situation to test.

Looking back, you might also realize you only tested straightforward
situations, and so you might think of something more difficult to try.

And finally, have another look at real requests, bug reports,
and recorded runs too.

There may be some useful examples you didn't include in your first
test set or new ones that have come up since.

Once you've chosen some situations worth testing,
look for real requests and records you can use in those cases,

because they help your test set reflect the situations your
application is actually encountering.

So you might look through cases from manual review, user requests,
bug reports, support tickets, or recorded runs,
starting with any examples you found while looking for gaps.

For example, you might find a support ticket for the shelter about an
experienced volunteer who wasn't eligible for outings.

The original request and volunteer record can give you the information
to use in your test.

Alternatively, if you can't find a real example of the situation you
want to test, you can write the request and records yourself,

or describe the situation you need to an LLM and ask it to fill in the
details for the case you've already chosen.
This is all very similar to when you put together your original cases,

so check that the requests and records describe the situation you
meant to test and that the details are realistic,
and write down what the application should do under the requirement.

Keep a note of where the information came from,
including anything you've created or changed.

Now, as you put these cases together, compare them with the
ones you already have.

Some may repeat a check you're already doing,
while others test a difference worth keeping.

For example, suppose you already have a shelter case where the
volunteer's experience is missing.

If another case only changes the volunteer's name,
you probably don't need both.

But a case where the dog's handling notes are missing checks
something different.

Handling missing volunteer information correctly doesn't tell you
whether the agent will also handle missing dog information correctly.

So both cases can be useful, even if they test the same requirement
and have the same expected outcome.

As you tune your test sets, remember each case takes work to
run and review again.
So think about what you'd stop checking if you left it out.

A useful case should either cover a meaningful situation,
protect against an important regression,
or clarify a boundary in the requirement.

You'll also want to review your existing cases to see
which ones you no longer need.

But be careful about removing a case just because you fixed a mistake,
because later changes could bring that mistake back.

There are good reasons to remove cases though,
such as when the shelter drops a rule that a case was testing.

And if a rule changes, but the case is still useful,
update what you expect the application to do.

And as you choose which cases to keep, make sure the important,
difficult situations get enough attention.

Because lots of straightforward cases can make the overall results
look good, even when the application struggles with difficult ones.

For example, suppose the agent passes 98 straightforward cases
but fails the only two difficult ones.
That's a 98% pass rate, even though it got both difficult cases wrong.
So look at the difficult cases separately,

and keep enough useful examples to see whether changes to the
application help with those situations.

Keep ordinary cases, too, so you can check that those changes don't
break something that already worked.

You can include more difficult cases than you'd normally see in
everyday use, so you have enough examples to check them.

Just remember that the overall score describes performance on the
benchmark you built,
not the true frequency of success or failure in production.

Together, those cases give you a benchmark that you can reuse
as you improve your application.

When you compare versions, use the same cases
and expected results for both,

so a change in the tests doesn't make one version look
better than the other.

In the next video, you'll apply the full benchmark workflow to
Northwind and see how the curated test set becomes the benchmark
you'll use in Module 3.
